rationales.B: Strictness is defined by the restrictions imposed and the degree of action required, not by the size of the sanction. A regime with heavy fines but a narrower duty is not the stricter one for purposes of Standard I(A).
rationales.C: The "more strict" law or regulation is the law or regulation that imposes greater restrictions on the action of the member or candidate, or that calls for the member or candidate to exert a greater degree of action to protect the interests of clients. Applicable law is the law that governs the member's or candidate's conduct, and which law applies depends on the particular facts and circumstances of each case.

questions.stem: Under Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law, members and candidates most likely must:

options.A: comply with applicable laws and regulations related to their professional activities.
options.B: comply with the less strict of applicable law or the Code and Standards.
options.C: give precedence to applicable local law where it conflicts with the Code and Standards.

rationales.A: Standard I(A) sets out three principles. Members and candidates must comply with applicable laws or regulations related to their professional activities. They must not engage in conduct that constitutes a violation of the Code and Standards, even though it may otherwise be legal. And in the absence of any applicable law or regulation, or when the Code and Standards impose a higher degree of responsibility than applicable laws and regulations, they must adhere to the Code and Standards.
rationales.B: The principle runs the other way. Where applicable law and the Code and Standards differ, the member must satisfy the stricter of the two, so complying with the less strict of them leaves the higher duty unmet.
rationales.C: Local law does not automatically prevail. Members must comply with applicable law, but where the Code and Standards impose a higher degree of responsibility than that law, or where no law or regulation applies at all, the Code and Standards govern; conduct that is legal locally can still breach them.

questions.stem: When direct discussions with the person committing an ethical violation have been unsuccessful, the first intermediate step toward dissociation under Standard I(A) is most likely to:

options.A: abstain from the conduct personally, with no further step required.
options.B: bring the behavior to the attention of a supervisor or compliance.
options.C: resign from the firm immediately, without any prior escalation.

rationales.A: Inaction combined with continuing association with those involved in illegal or unethical conduct may be construed as participation or assistance in that conduct. Abstaining personally while remaining silent and attached to the activity is therefore not dissociation; the member must first attempt to stop the behavior and then step away from it.
rationales.B: Members and candidates may take intermediate steps to dissociate from the ethical violations of others when direct discussions with the person or persons committing the violation are unsuccessful. The first step is to attempt to stop the behavior by bringing it to the attention of the employer, through a supervisor or the firm's compliance department. If that attempt is unsuccessful, the member or candidate has a responsibility to step away and dissociate from the activity. Dissociation practices differ on the basis of the member's or candidate's professional role or responsibilities, and may include removing one's name from written reports or recommendations, asking for a different assignment, or refusing to accept a new client or to continue to advise a current client.
rationales.C: Escalation to a supervisor or to the compliance department comes first, and dissociation short of leaving is usually available: removing one's name from a report or recommendation, asking for a different assignment, or declining to accept or continue with the client. Leaving the employer is a last resort, not the only recognized method.

questions.stem: With respect to potential violations of the Code and Standards committed by fellow members and candidates, reporting those violations is most likely:

options.A: strongly encouraged by CFA Institute.
options.B: prohibited as a breach of loyalty to colleagues.
options.C: required in all cases.

rationales.A: CFA Institute strongly encourages members and candidates to report potential violations of the Code and Standards committed by fellow members and candidates. Although a failure to report is less likely to be construed as a violation than a failure to dissociate from unethical conduct, the impact of inactivity on the integrity of the capital markets can be significant. The Code and Standards do not compel members and candidates to report violations to their governmental or regulatory organizations unless such disclosure is mandatory under applicable law, voluntary reporting of that kind often being referred to as whistle-blowing, but such disclosure may be prudent under certain circumstances, and members and candidates should consult their legal and compliance advisers for guidance.
rationales.B: Loyalty to colleagues never bars the reporting of potential Code violations. The duty of loyalty runs to the employer and does not extend to concealing another member's misconduct; reporting is encouraged precisely because inactivity can do significant damage to the integrity of the capital markets.
rationales.C: Reporting is strongly encouraged, not required. The Code and Standards compel disclosure to a governmental or regulatory organization only where such disclosure is mandatory under applicable law, so a blanket obligation to report every suspected violation overstates the duty.

questions.stem: A member helps create investment products that will be distributed in several countries. Under Standard I(A), the member is most likely:

options.A: Entitled to leave distribution-country rules to the local selling agents.
options.B: Bound by the laws of both the origination and the distribution countries.
options.C: Bound only by the law of the product's country of domicile.

rationales.A: The member's own compliance duty does not stop at the border of the product's home market. Those who create or maintain investment services or products must be mindful of where the services or products will be sold as well as where they originate, and the obligation to understand and comply with applicable law in the distribution markets rests on them. Relying on the local selling agent to know the local rules does not discharge that duty: the creator still has to undertake the due diligence needed to understand the several bodies of law that apply to cross-border business.
rationales.B: Standard I(A) guidance is explicit that members and candidates involved in creating or maintaining investment services or investment products must be mindful of where these services or products will be sold and their places of origination. Those responsible for providing the services, or for creating or providing the products, must understand and comply with applicable laws and regulations in all relevant jurisdictions, and must undertake the necessary due diligence when transacting cross-border business to understand the multiple applicable laws and regulations. Because transactions in global markets can leave genuine uncertainty about which laws or regulations apply when activity spans jurisdictions, members should seek appropriate guidance — the firm's compliance and legal departments, and legal counsel outside the organization where warranted — in order to gain a reasonable understanding of their responsibilities.
rationales.C: Domicile is only half of the test. The guidance pairs the place of origination with the places where the product will be sold, and requires compliance with applicable laws and regulations in all relevant jurisdictions. A product lawfully structured where it is domiciled can still be sold into a market whose rules the creator has failed to consider, which is the exposure Standard I(A) is directed at.

questions.stem: When dissociating from an activity that violates the Code and Standards, a member's most appropriate step is to:

options.A: Document the violation.
options.B: Avoid documenting it, to limit legal liability.
options.C: Notify a colleague verbally.

rationales.A: Standard I(A) compliance practices state that when dissociating from an activity that violates the Code and Standards, members and candidates should document the violation. The documentation creates a record supporting the member's position that appropriate steps were taken to separate from the unethical activity. It sits alongside the other expected steps: attempting to stop the conduct by bringing it to the attention of a supervisor or the compliance department, and, if that effort fails, stepping away from the activity. Inaction coupled with continuing association can itself be construed as participation in the violation.
rationales.B: Documentation is a recommended protective step, not a liability to be avoided. The record is what later demonstrates that the member separated from the violation rather than acquiesced in it. Declining to create one leaves the member's continued association with the activity unexplained, which is the greater exposure, and it does nothing to meet the guidance's expectation that the violation be documented.
rationales.C: A remark to a peer leaves no record and stops nothing. The guidance calls for documenting the violation and urging the firm to cease the conduct, normally by raising it with a supervisor or with compliance. A verbal notification to a colleague neither puts the firm on notice nor evidences that the member took appropriate steps to separate from the activity.

questions.stem: A firm is unwilling to permit dissemination of an adverse opinion about a corporate client. Under Standard I(B), the analyst should most appropriately:

options.A: Publish favorable research to preserve the client relationship.
options.B: Urge the firm to place the company on a restricted list.
options.C: Avoid restricted lists, which deny clients research coverage.

rationales.A: Issuing research the analyst does not believe, in order to protect a corporate client relationship, is the compromise of independence and objectivity that Standard I(B) exists to prevent. The pressure that an investment banking or corporate relationship places on a research opinion must be managed by changing what the firm distributes, not by changing the opinion. A favorable report written to preserve a relationship misleads every reader who relies on it.
rationales.B: Standard I(B) compliance practices provide that if the firm is unwilling to permit dissemination of adverse opinions about a corporate client, members and candidates should encourage the firm to remove the controversial company from its research universe and place it on a restricted list, so that the firm disseminates only factual information about the company. Restricted lists are a recognized tool for managing the conflicts inherent in investment banking relationships: a company subject to a potential offering can be placed on the list so that research is not issued under pressure, and the firm distributes facts rather than a recommendation it will not allow to be negative.
rationales.C: Withholding a recommendation is not the same as withholding coverage of the facts. A company on a restricted list still has factual information distributed about it; what stops is the issuance of an opinion the firm would not permit to be adverse. That is the remedy the guidance recommends precisely because the alternative — an opinion shaped by the banking relationship — is worse for clients than the absence of one.

questions.stem: When attending an analyst event hosted by an issuer, best practice for members under Standard I(B) is most likely to:

options.A: Accept issuer-paid charter flights whenever they save the firm money.
options.B: Reject special cost arrangements and pay their own travel and lodging.
options.C: Decline to attend issuer-sponsored events altogether.

rationales.A: Cost savings to the member's firm are not the test. Accepting a special cost arrangement from the subject company creates the appearance of a conflict regardless of who benefits from the saving, and corporate-sponsored air transportation is the clearest case: the guidance states that corporations should not reimburse members and candidates for air transportation. Where commercial transportation is unavailable, accepting the issuer's flight may be unavoidable, but it is the exception rather than a practice to be chosen for economy.
rationales.B: Standard I(B) compliance practices on restricting special cost arrangements state that when attending analyst events, best practice for members and candidates is to reject any special cost arrangements and to pay for their own commercial transportation and hotel charges. Acceptance of such arrangements may create the appearance of a conflict of interest, which is enough to impair the perceived independence of the research that follows, and corporations should not reimburse members and candidates for air transportation.
rationales.C: Attendance itself is useful and permitted; analyst events are a legitimate source of information about an issuer. The guidance is aimed at the cost arrangements attached to the event, not at the event, so the member attends and pays for the commercial transportation and hotel charges personally or through the firm.

questions.stem: A member's employer has no policy on accepting gifts. Under Standard I(B), the member's acceptance of gratuities and gifts is most likely:

options.A: Unlimited in value.
options.B: Prohibited unless compliance approves it in writing.
options.C: Limited to token items.

rationales.A: The absence of a firm policy does not remove the member's own obligation. Standard I(B) compliance practices require members and candidates to limit the acceptance of gratuities and gifts to token items even where the employer has no policy on the subject. The duty runs to the member personally, so a silent employer handbook leaves the token-item ceiling in place rather than lifting it.
rationales.B: Token items are permissible, and the guidance sets a ceiling on value rather than a blanket approval regime. Requiring written pre-approval for even a token gift overstates the standard, which does not preclude customary, ordinary business-related entertainment so long as its purpose is not to influence or reward the member or candidate.
rationales.C: Standard I(B) compliance practices on limiting gifts state that even if a member's or candidate's employer does not have a policy on accepting gifts, members and candidates must limit the acceptance of gratuities and gifts to token items. The standard does not preclude customary, ordinary business-related entertainment as long as its purpose is not to influence or reward the member or candidate; what it rules out is a benefit large enough to be capable of influencing independence and objectivity.

questions.stem: Before accepting a bonus or gift offered by a client, a member under Standard I(B) is most likely required to:

options.A: Disclose the benefit to the employer.
options.B: Reject the benefit outright.
options.C: Do nothing, since clients are not third parties.

rationales.A: Standard I(B) guidance provides that prior to accepting bonuses or gifts from clients, members and candidates should disclose to their employers the benefits offered by those clients. If notification is not possible before acceptance, members and candidates must disclose to their employer the benefits previously accepted from clients. Disclosure allows the employer to make an independent determination about the extent to which the gift may affect the member's or candidate's independence and objectivity — for instance, whether a performance-linked bonus from one client creates an incentive to favor that client's portfolio over others.
rationales.B: A gift from an existing client is treated differently from an inducement offered by a third party seeking to influence the member, because the client relationship and the duty of loyalty already exist. Such benefits are not banned outright: acceptance can be permissible, and the mechanism the standard relies on is disclosure to the employer rather than refusal.
rationales.C: Client gifts carry their own conflict. A benefit received from one client can bias the member toward that client at the expense of others, so the benefit should be disclosed to the employer — as best practice before acceptance, and necessarily afterward if advance notification was not possible — so the employer can assess the effect on independence and objectivity.

questions.stem: Under Standard I(B), credit rating agencies are most likely:

options.A: Subject to conflicts resembling those in investment banking relationships.
options.B: Reliable enough to use without independent validation.
options.C: Free of conflicts, since their analysts do not advise the firms they rate.

rationales.A: Standard I(B) guidance on credit rating agency opinions holds that the work of credit rating agencies raises concerns similar to those inherent in investment banking relationships. Analysts may face pressure to issue ratings at a specific level because of other services the agency sells to the same companies, notably advising on the development of structured products. The agencies therefore need to develop the firewalls and protections that allow their different business lines to operate independently, and users of their output should be mindful of the potential conflicts.
rationales.B: Because of the potential conflicts in the rating agency's own business model, members and candidates who use information provided by credit rating agencies should be mindful of those conflicts and may need to validate the rating independently. Treating a published rating as sufficient on its own substitutes another party's possibly compromised judgment for the member's required diligence.
rationales.C: The rating agency's analysts are not insulated from the agency's other business. The same agency may advise companies on the development of structured products while rating them, which creates pressure to issue ratings at a particular level — a conflict closely analogous to the one between research and investment banking, and the reason firewalls between business lines are expected.

questions.stem: Under Standard I(B), having research analysts work with investment bankers is most likely:

options.A: Prohibited in all circumstances.
options.B: Appropriate in all cases, since it enhances market efficiency.
options.C: Appropriate only when the conflicts are effectively managed.

rationales.A: The standard does not ban the collaboration. Guidance on investment banking relationships acknowledges that collaboration between research analysts and investment banking colleagues may benefit the firm and enhance market efficiency; what it requires is that firms carefully balance the conflicts of interest inherent in that collaboration, and that any conflict not avoided be disclosed under Standard VI(A).
rationales.B: The benefit to the firm and to market efficiency is real but conditional. Guidance states that having analysts work with investment bankers is appropriate only when the conflicts are adequately and effectively managed, so collaboration conducted without those controls is not made acceptable by its efficiency benefits.
rationales.C: Standard I(B) guidance on investment banking relationships states that although collaboration between research analysts and investment banking colleagues may benefit the firm and enhance market efficiency, it requires firms to carefully balance the conflicts of interest inherent in the collaboration. Having analysts work with investment bankers is appropriate only when the conflicts are adequately and effectively managed, and any such conflict that is not avoided must be disclosed under Standard VI(A), Avoid or Disclose Conflicts.

questions.stem: Under Standard I(B), a member representing a firm that is trying to win an external management mandate is most likely:

options.A: Outside the standard's scope, which binds the selecting party.
options.B: Required to maintain independence and objectivity, as the selector is.
options.C: Free to set objectivity aside, as a marketer rather than an adviser.

rationales.A: Standard I(B) reaches both sides of the manager selection process, not only the side making the choice. It applies to gift givers as well as gift receivers, so a member seeking to be selected is squarely within its scope and must not attempt to compromise the objectivity of the person making the selection through gifts, benefits, or other considerations.
rationales.B: Members and candidates may find themselves on either side of the manager selection process: they can be involved in selecting external managers to receive portions of the firm's or a client's assets to manage, or they can represent their own firm in trying to be selected to manage an external client's assets. Both sides of the process must maintain their independence and objectivity so that decisions are made in the best interest of the firm's or the client's assets. The member seeking the mandate must not attempt to compromise the objectivity of the person making the selection by offering gifts, benefits, or other considerations, just as the selector must not accept them.
rationales.C: Marketing a mandate is not an exemption. Those seeking selection must not attempt to compromise the selector's objectivity through gifts, benefits, or other considerations, because the selection decision has to be made in the best interest of the assets being allocated. Treating the pitch as pure salesmanship is how inducements enter the process, which is the conduct the standard prohibits on the giving side.

questions.stem: A member publishes content online and through social media. Under Standard I(C), the member is most likely required to:

options.A: Monitor the content regularly to keep it current.
options.B: Do nothing further, as the platform assumes responsibility.
options.C: Complete a single compliance review at the time of posting.

rationales.A: Standard I(C) compliance practices state that members and candidates should regularly monitor materials and content posted online or through social media to ensure that they contain current information. Members and candidates who publish content through websites should also ensure that all reasonable precautions have been taken to protect the website's integrity, confidentiality, and security, and that the site does not misrepresent any information and provides full disclosure. Material that was accurate when posted can become a misrepresentation simply by remaining up after the facts change.
rationales.B: Responsibility for the accuracy and currency of a member's professional content stays with the member, whatever platform carries it. The hosting service does not assume the duty not to misrepresent, and the member is expected to monitor the posted material and to take reasonable precautions over the integrity, confidentiality, and security of a site under the member's control.
rationales.C: A review at the moment of posting cannot catch the problem the guidance is aimed at. Content that was accurate when published becomes stale as prices, holdings, credentials, or performance figures change, so the expectation is regular monitoring of posted materials to ensure they remain current, not a single check at publication.

questions.stem: Under Standard I(C), the recommended practice for avoiding plagiarism most likely includes:

options.A: maintaining copies of all materials relied on in preparing a report.
options.B: attributing quotations generically to leading analysts and experts.
options.C: keeping copies of one's own final published reports only.

rationales.A: Standard I(C) Avoiding Plagiarism sets out three compliance practices. Maintain copies: keep copies of all research reports, articles containing research ideas, material with new statistical methodologies, and other materials that were relied on in preparing the research report. Attribute quotations: attribute to their sources any direct quotations, including projections, tables, statistics, model and product ideas, and new methodologies prepared by persons other than recognized financial and statistical reporting services or similar sources. Attribute summaries: attribute to their sources any paraphrases or summaries of material prepared by others. Retaining everything relied on is therefore one of the listed steps, and it is the step that makes the other two verifiable after the fact.
rationales.B: Generic attribution without naming the source is itself an improper practice under the plagiarism guidance. The standard requires that direct quotations, projections, tables, statistics, model and product ideas, and new methodologies be attributed to their actual sources; a vague reference to 'leading analysts and investment experts' identifies no source and so does not satisfy the attribution requirement.
rationales.C: The guidance lists several steps rather than one: maintain copies of the source materials relied on, attribute direct quotations to their sources, and attribute paraphrases and summaries of material prepared by others. Keeping copies of one's own final published reports addresses neither the retention of the underlying source materials nor either attribution obligation, so it is not the whole of what Standard I(C) recommends.

questions.stem: Under Standard I(C), unintentional misrepresentation of qualifications and services is most likely prevented by:

options.A: understanding the limits of the firm's and one's own capabilities.
options.B: avoiding written summaries of firm qualifications.
options.C: leaving marketing descriptions to each employee without central review.

rationales.A: Members and candidates can prevent unintentional misrepresentations of the qualifications or services they or their firms provide if each member and candidate understands the limit of the firm's or individual's capabilities and the need to be accurate and complete in presentations. Whether or not their employer provides guidance, members and candidates must make certain that they understand the services the firm performs and its qualifications, and must disclose that information without misrepresentation. Each member and candidate should also prepare a summary of his or her own qualifications and experience and a list of the services he or she is capable of performing. This is the compliance practice on description of qualifications and services under Standard I(C).
rationales.B: Maintained written descriptions are the recommended practice, not a discouraged one: each member and candidate should prepare a summary of his or her own qualifications and experience and a list of the services he or she is capable of performing. Staleness is managed by keeping those descriptions current, not by declining to write them.
rationales.C: Understanding, and working from, the firm's prepared description of its qualifications and services is what prevents unintentional misrepresentation. An unreviewed description drafted by each employee invites exactly the overstatement of firm capabilities the standard is meant to prevent, since members must make certain that they understand the services the firm performs and its qualifications and disclose that information without misrepresentation.

questions.stem: With respect to third-party information, Standard I(C) most likely provides that members and candidates:

options.A: may present third-party research as their own if the source is a recognized firm.
options.B: must exercise care and diligence when incorporating third-party information.
options.C: bear no responsibility for misrepresentations in third-party materials they use.

rationales.A: Members and candidates must disclose their intended use of external third parties and must not represent the work of others as their own. The standing of the source does not change that: incorporating outside research without attribution is a misrepresentation whichever firm produced it.
rationales.B: Members and candidates must exercise care and diligence when incorporating third-party information into their own work. Misrepresentations that result from using materials produced by outside parties become the responsibility of members and candidates when they incorporate that material into or make it part of their work. When providing information to clients from third parties, members and candidates share a responsibility for the accuracy of the marketing and distribution materials that pertain to the third party's capabilities, services, and products. They must also disclose their intended use of external third parties and must not represent the work of others as their own. This is the Standard I(C) guidance on use of third-party information.
rationales.C: Misrepresentations that result from using materials produced by outside parties become the responsibility of members and candidates once that material is incorporated into or made part of their own work, which is precisely why care and diligence are required before it is used. Responsibility for the accuracy of marketing and distribution materials describing a third party's capabilities, services, and products is likewise shared, not disclaimed.

questions.stem: Regarding the selection of performance benchmarks, Standard I(C) most likely holds that:

options.A: the selection process is an area where misrepresentation may occur.
options.B: an appropriate benchmark must always accompany performance results.
options.C: any widely recognized market index is an acceptable benchmark.

rationales.A: The performance benchmark selection process is another area where misrepresentations may occur. Members and candidates may misrepresent the success of their performance record by presenting benchmarks that are not comparable to their strategies, and clients can be misled if the benchmark's results are not reported on a basis comparable to that of the fund's or client's results. Best practice is selecting the most appropriate available benchmark from the universe of available options, and transparent presentation of appropriate performance benchmarks gives clients information useful for investment decisions. Where a reference index such as a 'cash plus' basis is used for a hedge fund, the reasons behind using that reference index must be disclosed. This is the Standard I(C) guidance on investment performance.
rationales.B: Standard I(C) does not require that a benchmark always be provided in order to comply. Some investment strategies may not lend themselves to displaying an appropriate benchmark because of the complexity or diversity of the investments included. The obligation is to select the most appropriate available benchmark where one exists, to report it on a comparable basis, and to disclose the reasons for a reference index that is not a conventional benchmark.
rationales.C: Presenting a benchmark that is not comparable to the strategy misrepresents the success of a performance record, and clients are misled when the benchmark's results are not reported on a basis comparable to the fund's or client's results. Best practice is selecting the most appropriate available benchmark from the universe of available options, and wide recognition of an index does not by itself make it comparable to the strategy being reported.

questions.stem: With respect to pricing illiquid or non-traded securities, Standard I(C) most likely holds that:

options.A: such securities raise no misrepresentation concerns.
options.B: the highest reputable valuation available may be reported.
options.C: reporting misrepresentations may occur when several valuations exist.

rationales.A: Valuation uncertainty heightens rather than removes the misrepresentation risk the guidance addresses. It is precisely because illiquid and non-traded securities can be valued from more than one source that members and candidates must take reasonable steps to provide accurate and reliable security pricing information to clients on a consistent basis.
rationales.B: Shopping among sources for the most favorable value may misrepresent a security's worth, lead to misinformed decisions to sell or hold the investment, and result in overcharging clients for advisory fees. Changing pricing providers must not be based solely on the justification that the new provider reports a higher current value of a security, so the standing of the provider does not cure a selection made for its favorable result; the selection must be consistent and justified.
rationales.C: Reporting misrepresentations may also occur when valuations for illiquid or non-traded securities are available from more than one source. When different options are available, members and candidates may be tempted to switch providers to obtain higher security valuations. The process of shopping for values may misrepresent a security's worth, lead to misinformed decisions to sell or hold the investment, and result in overcharging clients for advisory fees. Members and candidates must take reasonable steps to provide accurate and reliable security pricing information to clients on a consistent basis, and changing pricing providers must not be based solely on the justification that the new provider reports a higher current value of a security. Consistency in the valuation process improves the value of the security pricing information. This is the Standard I(C) guidance.

questions.stem: Regarding omissions in the use of models and in performance reporting, Standard I(C) most likely holds that:

options.A: omitting a fact or outcome can be misleading.
options.B: the best-performing accounts may represent a strategy.
options.C: model outputs may be presented as factual results.

rationales.A: The omission of a fact or outcome can be misleading, especially in the use of models and technical analysis processes. When inputs are knowingly omitted, the resulting outcomes may provide misleading information to those who rely on that information for making investment decisions. Outcomes from models must not be presented as fact, because they represent the expected results based on the inputs and analysis process incorporated. Omissions in the performance measurement and attribution process can also misrepresent a manager's performance and skill, and members and candidates must not misrepresent performance history by engaging in practices that distort past investment performance, such as cherry-picking the highest-performing accounts and presenting them as representative of a strategy. This is the Standard I(C) guidance on omissions.
rationales.B: Cherry-picking the highest-performing accounts and presenting them as representative of a strategy distorts past investment performance and misrepresents a manager's performance and skill, even where every reported return is accurate, because the selection itself omits the accounts that would show the strategy's actual result.
rationales.C: Outcomes from models must not be presented as fact, because they represent the expected results based on the inputs and the analysis process incorporated. Where inputs are knowingly omitted, the resulting outcomes may provide misleading information however objective the remaining inputs appear.

questions.stem: Beyond ensuring their own conduct complies, members and candidates under Standard I(D) are most likely expected to:

options.A: encourage their firms to adopt a code of ethics.
options.B: confine their attention to their own individual behavior.
options.C: leave organizational deterrence to the compliance function.

rationales.A: In addition to ensuring that their own behavior is consistent with Standard I(D), to prevent general misconduct members and candidates should encourage their firms to adopt a code of ethics to which every employee must subscribe, and to make clear that any personal behavior that reflects poorly on the individual involved, the institution as a whole, or the investment industry will not be tolerated. This is the compliance practice recommended under Standard I(D).
rationales.B: The guidance says members and candidates should encourage their firms to adopt a code of ethics and to make clear that behavior reflecting poorly on the individual, the institution, or the industry will not be tolerated. The expectation therefore extends past one's own behavior to the firm-level measures that deter general misconduct.
rationales.C: Individual conduct obligations and firm-level encouragement operate together. Standard I(D) asks members and candidates themselves to press for a firm code of ethics to which every employee subscribes, so deterring misconduct at the organizational level is not left entirely to a compliance function.

questions.stem: Under Standard I(D), the definition of a professional activity most likely turns on:

options.A: the nature of the conduct and its link to the profession.
options.B: whether the task was performed for pay at the current employer.
options.C: whether the conduct is direct portfolio management for clients.

rationales.A: A professional activity is any activity or conduct that relates to financial analysis, investment management, security analysis, stewardship, or other similar professional endeavors and either (1) involves activity or conduct in the workplace or academia or participation in the investment profession or security markets, or (2) explicitly or implicitly encompasses the use of the CFA charter or CIPM designation, membership in CFA Institute or CFA Institute local societies, or candidacy for a designation sponsored by CFA Institute. The test is thus the character of the conduct together with its connection to the profession or to CFA Institute credentials. This is the Standard I(D) guidance.
rationales.B: The definition turns on the nature of the activity, namely financial analysis, investment management, security analysis, stewardship, and similar professional endeavors, rather than on employment or pay. Conduct while working as an unpaid officer, representative, or volunteer with CFA Institute or a local society falls within it, as does conduct in academia and conduct that implicitly invokes the charter or candidacy.
rationales.C: Security analysis, stewardship, and other similar professional endeavors are expressly within the definition, and activity or conduct in academia is named in the standard's own examples, so the reach is considerably wider than direct portfolio management for clients.

questions.stem: Under Standard I(D), interactions with colleagues and employees are most likely:

options.A: excluded, since only client-facing interactions qualify.
options.B: included, in the workplace, in academia, or in the profession.
options.C: excluded whenever they occur away from the office.

rationales.A: Interactions with colleagues and employees are listed alongside interactions with clients among the examples of professional activities, so the standard is not confined to client-facing conduct.
rationales.B: Examples of conduct by members and candidates considered professional activities under Standard I(D) include, but are not limited to, the following: interactions with colleagues, employees, or clients in the workplace or academia or when participating in the investment profession; activities in which a member or candidate represents to others that he or she is a CFA charterholder, a candidate for a designation sponsored by CFA Institute, or a CFA Institute member; conduct while working as an unpaid officer, representative, or volunteer with CFA Institute or a local society; conduct while attending or participating in a CFA Institute, local society, or industry-related meeting, course, conference, or event; writing about investments or the markets in articles, books, reports, message boards, or blogs outside the workplace or academia; and communicating with a government agency, regulator, or other professional organization regarding information within the scope of the member's or candidate's professional responsibilities related to the investment profession.
rationales.C: Interactions with colleagues and employees when participating in the investment profession are included wherever they occur, and the examples reach conduct at an industry-related meeting, course, conference, or event, in academia, and in writing outside the workplace. Being away from the office therefore does not place such conduct beyond the standard.

questions.stem: A member's personal bankruptcy filing under Standard I(D) is most likely:

options.A: a violation only if the circumstances involve deceitful conduct.
options.B: incapable of implicating the Code and Standards.
options.C: a violation in every case.

rationales.A: Personal bankruptcy may not reflect on the integrity or trustworthiness of the person declaring bankruptcy, but if the circumstances of the bankruptcy involve fraudulent or deceitful business conduct, the bankruptcy may be a violation of this standard. The determination depends on the facts and circumstances surrounding the filing rather than on the filing itself. This is the Standard I(D) guidance.
rationales.B: Bankruptcy is a lawful remedy, but where its circumstances involve fraudulent or deceitful business conduct the standard is implicated. The legality of the filing does not insulate the conduct that led to it from review under the Code and Standards.
rationales.C: Personal bankruptcy alone may not reflect on the integrity or trustworthiness of the person declaring it, so a filing is not a violation in itself. A violation arises only where the surrounding circumstances involve fraudulent or deceitful business conduct, which is a facts-and-circumstances determination.

questions.stem: Regarding the CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program, the most likely accurate statement is that:

options.A: enforcement action is guaranteed once a complaint is filed.
options.B: some individuals abuse it to settle disputes unrelated to professional ethics.
options.C: filing a complaint against another member is discouraged.

rationales.A: A complaint triggers a review by Professional Conduct staff; it does not guarantee that enforcement action follows. Nothing in the Code and Standards promises a particular outcome, and a complaint pressed in bad faith is itself misconduct.
rationales.B: Standard I(D) guidance notes that individuals may attempt to abuse the CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program by actively seeking CFA Institute enforcement of the Code and Standards, and in particular Standard I(D), as a method of settling personal, political, or other disputes unrelated to professional ethics. CFA Institute is aware of this issue, and appropriate disciplinary policies, procedures, and enforcement mechanisms are in place to address misuse of the Code and Standards and of the Professional Conduct Program in this way.
rationales.C: Reporting suspected violations is encouraged rather than discouraged. What the guidance warns against is bad-faith use of the program, meaning complaints filed to settle personal, political, or other disputes unrelated to professional ethics.

questions.stem: Under Standard I(E), the guidance on achieving and maintaining competence most likely indicates that:

options.A: only formal university coursework maintains competence.
options.B: outside reading of industry publications is excluded.
options.C: a continuing education or professional development program qualifies.

rationales.A: Many pathways qualify, not formal coursework alone: professional development and continuing education programs, studying for or earning certifications and designations, conferences and seminars, employer training, informal self-study, and participation in expert groups.
rationales.B: Outside reading of subject matter articles, treatises, and publications is expressly listed as a form of informal continuing education or self-study, so such reading is recognized rather than excluded as insufficiently rigorous.
rationales.C: Standard I(E) compliance practices list the activities members and candidates should consider in order to achieve and maintain competence: regularly engaging in a professional development or continuing education program; studying for or earning professional certifications or designations; attending conferences, seminars, or webinars; regularly participating in training offered by their employer; diligently engaging in informal continuing education or self-study, such as outside reading of subject matter articles, treatises, and publications; participating in expert groups or organizations; and becoming proficient with any new skill or knowledge, as necessary, when their professional responsibilities change.

questions.stem: Under Standard I(E), the duty with respect to continuing education most likely:

options.A: requires annual completion of the CFA Institute Professional Learning program.
options.B: mandates no particular continuing education program or development plan.
options.C: requires a fixed number of certified continuing education hours each year.

rationales.A: No particular program or provider is mandated by the standard. Standard I(E) contemplates ongoing professional development but leaves the means to the member or candidate, so completing any one specified program each year is not a requirement of the standard.
rationales.B: Although Standard I(E) contemplates ongoing professional development to maintain proficiency and competence, the standard does not mandate participation in a particular continuing education program or professional development plan. Members and candidates can attain and maintain the competence needed to fulfill their professional responsibilities in a variety of ways.
rationales.C: The standard contemplates ongoing development without prescribing hour counts, annual certification, or any other fixed measure of continuing education as a condition of membership.

questions.stem: Under Standard I(E), the guidance on knowledge, skills, and abilities most likely holds that:

options.A: knowledge is information applied directly to performing a function.
options.B: skills are theoretical information and knowledge is applied technique.
options.C: the three terms are synonymous and used interchangeably.

rationales.A: Knowledge is the body of information applied directly to the performance of a function and how effectively it is applied. Skills are capabilities to perform a role-specific act or function to complete specific tasks and achieve professional goals. Abilities are capabilities and attitudes that support behaviors that result in observable outcomes.
rationales.B: That reverses the two definitions. Knowledge is the body of information applied directly to the performance of a function and how effectively it is applied, while skills are the capabilities to perform a role-specific act or function in order to complete specific tasks and achieve professional goals.
rationales.C: The guidance defines the three terms distinctly: knowledge as applied information, skills as role-specific capabilities to complete tasks and achieve professional goals, and abilities as capabilities and attitudes that support behaviors resulting in observable outcomes. They are not interchangeable.

questions.stem: Standard I(E) guidance on the competence of a member or candidate most likely indicates that:

options.A: a member's education level establishes competence for any assignment.
options.B: competence is not limited to a member's education level.
options.C: competence in one practice area transfers to related areas.

rationales.A: Competence is not limited to an examination of education level. A highly educated investment consultant may lack the experience to undertake consulting activities in an unfamiliar area of practice, so formal education by itself does not establish competence for any assignment the member takes on.
rationales.B: Competence is not limited to an examination of the education level of a member or candidate. A highly educated investment consultant may not have the experience to undertake consulting activities in an unfamiliar area of practice. An accounting professional supremely competent in providing financial statement audits may not be competent in assessing compliance with performance presentation standards, such as the GIPS standards. An investment consultant hired to conduct a search for an investment manager focused on sustainable investing may not have the skills needed to competently evaluate managers with that focus.
rationales.C: Competence is role- and area-specific and does not transfer automatically. An accounting professional competent in financial statement audits may not be competent in assessing compliance with the GIPS standards, and a consultant may lack the skills to evaluate managers focused on sustainable investing.

questions.stem: When professional responsibilities change over time, Standard I(E) most likely requires that:

options.A: new duties be declined rather than met with new competence.
options.B: competence attained on entering the profession suffice for a career.
options.C: new or different knowledge, skills, and abilities be acquired.

rationales.A: The expected response is extending competence, not refusing growth in responsibility. Members and candidates develop and refine their skills and abilities as their careers progress, becoming proficient with new skills or knowledge as their professional responsibilities change.
rationales.B: Over time professional responsibilities may change or expand, requiring new or different knowledge, skills, and abilities, so the competence attained on entering the profession does not remain sufficient for an entire career.
rationales.C: Over time, the professional responsibilities of members and candidates may change or expand, requiring new or different knowledge, skills, and abilities. Members and candidates will develop and refine their skills and abilities as their careers progress. Standard I(E) imposes the duty to not simply achieve but also maintain competence, emphasizing the need for members to continuously maintain or improve the competence required of their professional position.
